items.text:
The Legend Of Zelda: Trails Of Time Officially Unveiled

Published Sep 28, 2026, 5:42 AM EDT

James is a gaming writer from London who has spent thousands of hours exploring titles from every genre. Though he has a particular affinity for multiplayer titles like World of Warcraft, Destiny 2 and League of Legends, he has also put thousands of hours into single-player experiences, from deep RPGs to epic PC strategies. When he's not playing or writing, he can usually be found supporting his beloved Brentford FC.

The Legend of Zelda's 40th anniversary celebrations really have been a particularly happy time for the fan base as a whole, and while there were some concerns in the early portion of it, Nintendo has really delivered on marking it overall. There has obviously been the raft of announcements and confirmations that we received as part of the recent, dedicated Zelda Direct, which chiefly served the purpose of showing us a lot more of the upcoming movie adaptation, and the Ocarina of Time Remake which is scheduled to release in November.

Up to that point, the latter had remained a total mystery, with a teaser of just a few seconds showing Link asleep on his bed at the start of the game. Now, we know a lot more about what we'll be getting, with more emerging all the time from the developer themselves, including a new post that confirms a pretty major addition that should make the playing experience a lot more modern.

Over on Twitter/X, the official Japanese language profile for Zelda shared a post confirming a new feature that's set to be included in the Ocarina of Time Remake. The post reads as follows:

"This is a new feature that allows you to confirm your next objective or look back on your adventures so far. Additionally, as you progress through the adventure, a large tapestry painting gradually fills up."

It essentially sounds like it's going to function as an interactive adventure log, and a variation on the usual menus while still including the quality-of-life features that fans now expect. Plenty of fans weighed in to respond to the post with their own thoughts on the system, and overall it all seemed fairly popular.

"Trails of Time is like an adventure logbook, I suppose. The idea of a large tapestry painting is intriguing too. Like a group photo of the sages including Saria, akin to the Poem of the Heroes including the Hero and the Princess," one comment read.

While another added their thoughts on everything we have seen so far, saying, "The time-traveling makeup, the graphics are unbelievably gorgeous, and the level of detail in the crafting is incredible too! I just hope those dark elements like the blood-soaked Dead Hand or the blood at the bottom of the well don't get censored. It's the contrast between light and dark that makes this game so uniquely special, after all."

The Ocarina of Time Remake is set to launch on November 5, 2026, or exactly two weeks before the release of GTA VI, if that is how you're currently measuring everything at the moment. That should give you plenty to do in that final fortnight, before presumably half the gaming population is lost to the siren's song that Rockstar has been cooking up.

items.text:
Coffee first, opinions later. The Moon settles into Taurus early, craving comfort food and zero surprises. Too bad the Sun has other plans. Its trine with Uranus peaks today, tossing a lucky wild card into an otherwise ordinary Monday. The best idea of your day could come from the most random place, stargazer, so leave some room for it. Mars is settling into Leo and gearing up for a showdown with Pluto, while the Moon’s squares to both planets make tempers easy to spark. Saturn is beginning to oppose the Sun, testing how well your big plans hold up. Pick your battles, and save your ammo for the arguments you’d still defend next month.

Read your horoscope for the week, and see what the stars have in store for your sign today.

Aries: March 21 – April 19

Somebody’s going to cut in line at the coffee shop, and you’ll want to make it a whole production. Mars strolling into Leo gives you a fresh dose of swagger, Aries, while the Moon squaring it keeps your fuse short. Pour that heat into a project you’ve been itching to start. Uranus sextile Mars sneaks in an unexpected opening, so grab it with both hands.

Aries monthly horoscope

Taurus: April 20 – May 20

The Moon slides into your sign, and it’s like coming home to find someone already did the dishes. Pluto’s grip on Venus is loosening, so that possessive streak you’ve been nursing since mid-September can finally take a nap, Taurus. Stop refreshing their Instagram stories. Put that energy into something that loves you back, like a long lunch or the couch you paid good money for.

Taurus monthly horoscope

Gemini: May 21 – June 20

That joke you’re dying to drop in the work chat? Let it marinate. Mercury in Libra wants to charm everyone, Gemini, but Mars and Pluto are squaring it, which means people will hear an edge you never intended. Your best move is a phone call over a text. Tone travels better through an actual voice, and you’re more lovable when they can hear you laughing.

Gemini monthly horoscope

Cancer: June 21 – July 22

Your one boundary gets tested by someone’s Monday meltdown. The Moon leaves Aries for Taurus and wants you in sweatpants with a bowl of soup, but its squares to Mars and Pluto keep dragging other people’s drama to your door, Cancer. You’re allowed to hand it back. Offer sympathy without signing up for the rescue mission, then guard your evening like a lifeboat.

Cancer monthly horoscope

Leo: July 23 – August 22

Your weirdest idea is the right one, so pitch it before anybody talks you into beige. The Sun trines Uranus today, handing you a lucky streak of originality, Leo, while Mars rolls into your sign with a pep talk. Saturn is lining up to oppose the Sun soon, so take the green light while it’s glowing. No one ever built a legend by playing it safe.

Leo monthly horoscope

Virgo: August 23 – September 22

Someone’s going to vent to you, and your first instinct will be a color-coded action plan. Hold that thought, Virgo. Mercury in Libra is catching heat from Mars and Pluto, so even your kindest fix-it notes could come off as criticism. Ask if they want solutions or just someone on their side. Half the time, a well-timed “ugh, that sucks” does the job.

Virgo monthly horoscope

Libra: September 23 – October 22

When someone asks where to eat tonight, name an actual restaurant. The Sun in your sign is trining Uranus, which makes a surprise burst of decisiveness very on-brand, Libra. Pluto is loosening its hold on Venus, so you can ask for what you want in love without it feeling like a hostage negotiation. Start with dinner and work your way up to the bigger asks.

Libra monthly horoscope

Scorpio: October 23 – November 21

You’ll catch wind of something you weren’t supposed to hear, and your poker face is about to get a workout. Pluto is squaring Mercury and facing off with Mars, so information is currency today, Scorpio, and you’re holding a very good hand. Resist the urge to confront anyone just yet. Let them keep talking. People reveal the most when they think nobody’s keeping score.

Scorpio monthly horoscope

Sagittarius: November 22 – December 21

You’ve mentioned that pottery class at three happy hours, so maybe sign up already. Jupiter in Leo has no major aspects pulling at it today, Sagittarius, which leaves your ruling planet free to do what it does best and expand your horizons. With Mars now in Jupiter’s sign, there’s extra fire under your feet. Your friends are ready for an update that includes actual clay.

Sagittarius monthly horoscope

Weird Weekend

Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. Pop back every weekend to find out what Jeremy, Josh and Rick have become obsessed with this time, whether it's the canon height of Thief's Garrett or that time someone in the Vatican pirated Football Manager.

PC gaming, as a hobby, is a vast desert of inessentials. You want lights on your keyboard? Lights on your RAM? A graphics card that emits cherry vapour and has an anime lady on it? All these things and more can be yours, for the low price of an alarmingly high price.

But when I took a Gamescom appointment to check out the Scentbar, I felt like I was plumbing an entire new stratum of frippery. The pitch is simple: stick this miniature soundbar-ish thing on your desk, run a bit of software that detects what's happening on your screen, et voila, it will start kicking out stinks that match the action.

(Image credit: Future)This is, somehow, an idea that has been attempted several times before. But from reading my colleagues' reactions to those prior efforts, I get the impression they, ah, sucked.

So here are my two key takeaways from my Gamescom Scentbar demo: first, you absolutely, comprehensively, definitively do not need to buy this thing and almost certainly should not. Second, I have to admit it works, to a degree I find myself impressed by essentially against my will.

Swing and a whiff

My demo of the Scentbar began in a bakery—a first-person perspective of someone (a baker, you have to assume) dashing around a cosy-game-coded space and rearranging croissants. This, happily, was quickly recognised by the Scentbar's AI-detection gubbins, which quickly began emitting a distinctly bakery-like odour.

(Image credit: Future)The hardware side of it works like this: the little soundbar thing that sits on your desk can be equipped with up to 10 cartridges, each of which is filled with a distinct set of scent pellets. For my demo, it was loaded with Forest, Grass, Pineapple, Flowers, Bakery, Sea, Farm, Garage, Smoke, and Gunpowder. Bakery, naturally, kicked in for the croissant-focused segments of the demonstration. When Salomo Bertram, the Scentbar boss who was showing this stuff off, started throwing bombs about in another game, the bar emitted gunpowder. In a car mechanic sim? Garage. You get it.

I do not know by what magic the world's scent-makers have produced a tiny white pellet that smells 100% like 'garage,' but they sure as hell have done, and the same goes for the rest of the Scentbar's arsenal of odours. Precisely how much the Scentbar AI has to 'recognise' what it's seeing before it starts spitting out a relevant smell is configurable by its software.

If you want, you can have it emit gunpowder at the merest hint of a weapon on screen, or you can set it to more-or-less require a notarised form from the government affirming the presence of gunplay before it even thinks about it. In this way, says Bertram, you can "set it up to your preferences and individualize your experience," but you can't add your own smells yet, due to "safety issues."

(Image credit: Future)Alas, Bertram had not brought his fish or faeces pellets with him to Gamescom, which meant I could not get direct experience of the Scentbar's capacity to produce foul smells. I did see/smell it accurately parse Minecraft's blocky forestry, though—correctly pumping out the smells of grass and fir trees as we swanned about in creative mode.

In a game called Lost Legion—which did not seem great—I got to inhale the scent of a burning Roman soldier as I stood the game's protagonist in a roaring brazier. Well, okay, I got the smell of fire. 'Burning flesh' was not loaded into the Scentbar and probably should never be.

You absolutely, definitely do not need a machine that lets you smell your games, and if a loved one ever came to me asking if they should pick one up, I would encourage them to fill whatever spiritual void had led to them asking me that question.

(Image credit: Future)Nevertheless.

I can't help but be rather impressed by the Scentbar. It's a patently ridiculous idea, but it's a patently ridiculous idea that does seem to function quite well. If you ever find yourself with a free half-hour at an enormous games industry convention, there are worse things you could do with it than check one out.

items.text:
As more and more game companies are growing a little bolder about just straight-up admitting that huge chunks of their games are AI generated, there are still some exhibiting a bit more caution. One of those appears to be Nippon Ichi Software, developer of Disgaea and publisher of series like Trails and Ys.

I spoke to Nippon Ichi CEO and NIS America president Kenzo Saruhashi at PAX West a few weeks ago, during which time I asked him about AI, first just as a follow-up to a question about translation and localization of the company’s games. Saruhashi was recently appointed president of NIS America in addition to his role as CEO of Nippon Ichi, and one of the aims of that is for the two branches of the company to become more unified and ultimately release more games in the West. Saruhashi told me this includes trying to release more games simultaneously worldwide, instead of delaying Western releases until months after they’re out in Japan. But doing that requires ramping up localization capabilities within the company.

Given the current climate, it might be tempting to jump to using generative AI for this sort of thing. Other companies are certainly talking big games about it lately, though at least in anime its use has been both wildly unpopular and also frequently very, very wrong. So I asked Saruhashi if the company was currently using AI for localization, and here’s what he said:

We are not specifically at the moment. But we are researching it, because we know that there are a lot of companies right now that are utilizing AI, and it’s not necessarily that we would just allow AI to completely take over the responsibility for localization or anything of that nature, but more in order to ensure the quality. We want to make sure that we can ensure the quality is there at the same time if we were to use it. So right now we’re in a researching phase to see whether that’s something that’s possible. Personally, I don’t think that it’s necessarily just that utilizing AI will necessarily make things faster.

I followed up: Does this philosophy apply to all aspects of his business? It seems it largely does:

Well, let me start by saying that I can definitely feel there’s a certain sense of pressure in the creative industry as a whole that we’re all feeling from AI. What I’m hearing a lot as I discussed this matter with other developers and hearing what they’re saying is really that for us, the end goal is really just to make a quality game for the fans. And in the midst of that, we can’t simply ignore AI entirely. And so we do at least have to research it as a possibility moving forward, and I agree with that sentiment. I think if you were to apply AI, the best way to do so would be in a way that actually improves the quality of the game, so we’re not just looking at it specifically from an efficiency standpoint. I don’t think that’s really the way to look at it. You should look at it as, “does it improve the quality of the end product?”

Admittedly, “researching” has, for many companies, been the very first step into full-on AI content creation, especially at Japanese game studios, so regard all this with some skepticism (still reeling from the Level-5 AI use over here!). But at least for now I can take a deep breath and give Village in the Shade a shot without worry.

Adam Blevins began working in the entertainment industry in 2022 as a Staff Writer for Agents of Fandom, where he progressed to Senior Editor and interviewed talent from Marvel Studios, House of the Dragon, and Planet of the Apes. He joined Collider as a News Author in April 2024, was promoted to a Senior position in December 2024, and has written over 3,000 articles for the site, including exclusives relating to Avengers: Doomsday, The Penguin, Star Wars: Skeleton Crew, and more. He primarily writes about the latest box office numbers and the hottest movies and TV shows on streaming, while also covering superhero and sci-fi news. He has completed a set visit for The Chosen and even has several months of experience writing Gaming Features at ScreenRant. You can find him on X, LinkedIn, and Muckrack.

When it comes to making great sci-fi movies, few directors are operating at the same level as James Cameron. The only few directors in the same air as Cameron are Ridley Scott, Christopher Nolan, and Steven Spielberg, but Cameron has added more to his career box office total than any of them except Spielberg. While Cameron’s work on the Avatar movies are the first that come to mind for modern audiences, he’s also famous for his work directing Titanic, which is the sixth-highest-grossing movie of all time. What makes this even more impressive is that it was released all the way back in 1997, so when factoring in inflation, it earned much more than just $2.2 billion. Cameron’s first Avatar movie is still the highest-grossing in history, with a lead of more than $100 million over Avengers: Endgame.

James Cameron took more than 10 years between the release of the first and second Avatar movies, but thanks to intense demand from fans, he was able to cut this gap down to just three years between the second and third films. Just one week before Christmas last year, James Cameron delivered Avatar: Fire and Ash into theaters around the world, and while the film failed to reach the same box office heights as either of its predecessors, it still grossed $1.48 billion at the box office, making it one of the highest-grossing movies in history. Avatar: Fire and Ash was added to Disney Plus earlier in the summer, where it has since found a home in the top 10 for 90 days now. It doesn’t look poised to give up its coveted streaming spot anytime soon, either.

Five universes. Five completely different ways the future went wrong — or sideways, or up in flames. Only one of them is the world your instincts were built for. Eight questions will figure out which dystopia, galaxy, or desert wasteland you'd actually make it out of alive.

01

You sense something is deeply wrong with the world around you. What do you do?
The first instinct is often the truest one.

APull on every thread until I understand the system — then figure out how to break it.
BStop asking questions and start stockpiling — food, fuel, weapons. Questions don't keep you alive.
CKeep my head down, observe carefully, and trust no one until I know who's pulling the strings.

02

In a world of scarcity, what resource do you guard most fiercely?
What we protect reveals what we believe survival actually requires.

AKnowledge. If you understand the system, you don't need resources — you can generate them.
BFuel. Everything else — movement, power, escape — runs on it.
CTrust. In a world of fakes and informants, a truly reliable ally is rarer than any commodity.
DWater. And after water, information — the two things empires are truly built on.
EShips and credits. The galaxy is big — you survive it by being able to move through it freely.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What kind of threat keeps you up at night?
Fear is useful data — if you're honest about what you're actually afraid of.

AThat reality itself is a lie — that everything I experience has been constructed to keep me compliant.
BA raid. No warning, no mercy — just the roar of engines and then nothing left.
CBeing identified. Once someone with power decides you're a problem, you're already out of time.
DBeing outmanoeuvred — losing a political game I didn't even know I was playing.
EThe Empire tightening its grip until there's nowhere left to run.

04

How do you deal with authority you don't trust?
Every dystopia has a power structure. Your approach to it determines everything.

ASubvert it from the inside — learn its rules well enough to weaponise them against it.
BIgnore it and stay out of its reach. The further from any power structure, the better.
CAppear to comply while doing exactly what I need to do. Visibility is the enemy.
DManoeuvre within it carefully. You can't beat a system you refuse to understand.
EResist openly when I have to. Some things are worth the risk of being seen.

05

Survival isn't just tactical — it's physical, psychological, and very much about where you are.

AUnderground bunkers and server rooms — cramped, artificial, but with access to everything that matters.
BOpen wasteland — brutal sun, no shelter, constant movement. At least the threat is honest.
CA dense, rain-soaked city where you can disappear into the crowd and nobody asks questions.
DMerciless desert — extreme heat, no water, and something enormous living beneath the sand.
EThe fringe — backwater planets and busy spaceports where the Empire's attention rarely reaches.

06

Who do you want in your corner when things fall apart?
The company you keep is the clearest signal of who you actually are.

AA tight crew of believers who've seen behind the curtain and have nothing left to lose.
BOne or two people I'd trust with my life. Any more than that and someone talks.
CNobody, ideally. Alliances are liabilities. I work alone unless I have no choice.

5 Survival Games On Steam That Are Totally Free To Play

Updated
Sep 28, 2026, 6:56 AM EDT

James is a gaming writer from London who has spent thousands of hours exploring titles from every genre. Though he has a particular affinity for multiplayer titles like World of Warcraft, Destiny 2 and League of Legends, he has also put thousands of hours into single-player experiences, from deep RPGs to epic PC strategies. When he's not playing or writing, he can usually be found supporting his beloved Brentford FC.

Just as horror games put people in situations where they can experience immense scares from the safety and comfort of their own rooms, survival games do something similar. Sometimes its nice to fend for yourself without the genuinely high risk of death, and if you are a fan of the genre, there are few better places to go than Steam.

The platform has obviously become the premier option for anyone looking to play PC games, and the survival genre is no exception. Even better than that, there are some great options out there that don't even require you to spend any money, so we have rounded up five of the best into a handy list, so you can start making plans for next weekend.

Once Human

NetEase Games

Arguably the game that drew the most attention at launch on this list, Once Human might not be as popular as it once was, but there is still a genuinely solid survival game here. Set in a post-apocalyptic alternate future where monstrous enemies roam free, the game features some of the best base building around, as well as hundreds of ways to customize weapons, and deep survival mechanics that can quickly leave you in the dirt.

Fallout Shelter

The lesser-appreciated cousin of the mainline single-player games, Fallout Shelter allows players to run their very own vault, complete with all of the problems that come with that. Raiders will attack, food issues will occur and you might even have problems from within, all as you desperately struggle to create a home in the nuclear wasteland.

Unturned

Staggeringly created by solo developer Nelson Sexton at the frankly ridiculous age of just 16, Unturned is an open world zombie survival sandbox game built in Unity. You choose your skills and are thrust into a map with just your clothes, and from there you'll have to manage health, food, water, oxygen and radiation levels, all while dodging zombie attacks as you try to survive. Lighter than some of the other options on this list, it might have the most charm on this list.

Muck

Dani

Muck is a very different option than most in that it's a survival roguelike where the emphasis is on short play sessions, rather than continually building on your save for months. It comes with all of the usual survival fare, so you can craft, build, fight, and grow your character, all while exploring an island filled with a genuinely impressive array of foes.

No More Room In Hell

For those of you who prefer the more hardcore side of the survival spectrum, No More Room In Hell may well be the best pick for you. Originally built in the Source Engine (technically as a mod), the game takes inspiration from George Romero's "Of the Dead" series. As such, you can expect plenty of zombies who all think you look delicious and plenty of other hazards, all while trying to keep your base alive in the game's survival mode.

Even better than that, there are some great options out there that don't even require you to spend any money, so we have rounded up five of the best into a handy list, so you can start making plans for next weekend.
Once Human
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/once-human.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2

Arguably the game that drew the most attention at launch on this list, Once Human might not be as popular as it once was, but there is still a genuinely solid survival game here. Set in a post-apocalyptic alternate future where monstrous enemies roam free, the game features some of the best base building around, as well as hundreds of ways to customize weapons, and deep survival mechanics that can quickly leave you in the dirt.
Fallout Shelter
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/fallout-shelter-bunker.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2

The lesser-appreciated cousin of the mainline single-player games, Fallout Shelter allows players to run their very own vault, complete with all of the problems that come with that. Raiders will attack, food issues will occur and you might even have problems from within, all as you desperately struggle to create a home in the nuclear wasteland.
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F63128fee59bc0-ProfilePic.jpg?fit=crop&w=90&h=90
Unturned
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/unturned.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2

Staggeringly created by solo developer Nelson Sexton at the frankly ridiculous age of just 16, Unturned is an open world zombie survival sandbox game built in Unity. You choose your skills and are thrust into a map with just your clothes, and from there you'll have to manage health, food, water, oxygen and radiation levels, all while dodging zombie attacks as you try to survive. Lighter than some of the other options on this list, it might have the most charm on this list.
Muck
https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/muck.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
Dani

Muck is a very different option than most in that it's a survival roguelike where the emphasis is on short play sessions, rather than continually building on your save for months. Originally built in the Source Engine (technically as a mod), the game takes inspiration from George Romero's "Of the Dead" series. As such, you can expect plenty of zombies who all think you look delicious and plenty of other hazards, all while trying to keep your base alive in the game's survival mode.

items.author: Zack Kotzer
items.summary: My first campaign in Thousand Hells: The Underworld Heists, the new game from King of Dragon Pass creator David Dunham, went surprisingly smoothly. The queen
items.text:
My first campaign in Thousand Hells: The Underworld Heists, the new game from King of Dragon Pass creator David Dunham, went surprisingly smoothly. The queen of the Eternal City hired me to recover two princes, slain by their uncle, from the nether realm. Despite being challenged by mercenaries, giant spiders and a poetry battle, my entire crew emerged from the world below unscathed. Albeit with only one prince in tow.

“Just for my curiosity, were you playing on a Steam Deck?” Dunham asked me on a call. I was. Apparently my first-time win was flagged on the developer’s end. An illustration of how lucky I really was. And don’t worry. The campaigns that followed were far more turbulent. By the third encounter in my second descent, I had already pissed off the god of the raging ocean.

From 1999, King of Dragon Pass is a cult classic RPG. In essence a kingdom management game, it is expressed solely through story prompts. Instead of balancing gold and resources, the fate of your people is decided by your decisions. The weight of King Solomon’s guiding hand on each prompt. By comparison, Thousand Hells is more straightforward adventure book experience. In this game you’re just looking after numero uno. Numero cinco at most. While streamlined, it doesn’t sacrifice depth or detail, as each campaign presents an ornate and unpredictable journey into death and beyond.

This underworld is ever shifting in nature. Inspired by a stew of early civilizational beliefs, you must prepare for anything. At the start of each campaign, you’ll select your own traits and three additional crew members, who can range from surly lockpicks to nimble academics. Their class and characteristics introduce their own set of tiles, representing actions and ideas that can be called upon to deal with new situations. You will task one character to lead in each encounter, though they’ll have the ability to pull a few tiles from other crew members. You can imagine how much I was kicking myself when, standing before a mechanized door, my troublesome thief ready to take the bat, I accidentally clicked on the philosopher. A choice I had to live with, among all others. No take-backsies in the afterlife.

You may not see the immediate value in squading with sailors or poets initially, but the laws below are not the same as those above. In hell, words and stories can bend granite. Dry chunnels flow into raging seas if that seems like a fitting punishment. Despite my initial success, I suffered. My crew suffered. Yours will suffer. Campaigns usually last 40 minutes to an hour. With seemingly endless permutations, you’ll be dusting your knees off plenty of times.

You may have to curry favor with gods, big and demi. You may need to interrogate shades to safely navigate the sprawling labyrinths. Fend back packs of howling beasts. Blend in with marching armies. Outwit ghouls whose curses mix ancient hauntings with more modern folklore or Junji Ito-ian talltales. You will almost assuredly need to temper the emotions of your team, easily made manic from exposure to a place with no formal shape. If your hires warn you that they’re no fans of alcohol, insects or seducing demons, Dunham told me that at least one of them will likely come to fruition. Personally, it seems like an ominous thing to say out loud before plunging into hell, unless that demon kissing guy was attempting reverse psychology.

Dragon Pass exercised the power of words to shape a defiant kingdom. While your headcount is much smaller in Thousand Hells, the power of your words are two-fold. The undefined underworld presents a place where semiotics can rule supreme. The signified and signifier vying for power. Where irony takes precedent over hard physics. And whether you’re attempting to reshape the balance of power for the living, or hoping to plunder that one treasure that got away, how you tell your own story can quickly spiral into a hell of your own making.

items.text:
The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

Sundays are for recovering from the friend-of-a-spouse’s wedding you attended on Saturday while suffering from an acute case of Old Person’s Back. Unfortunately, the time for recovery has in fact passed, as you have already moved to the more immediately satisfying phase of assigning blame. Possible suspects: your swivel chair, your mattress, the PC monitor you had to laboriously re-box for transit, your sofa, and that most connviving, spine-bending bastard of all, light walking. Spoiled for choice, you sit down in your untrustworthy chair and begin to read some of the week’s writing highlights instead.

Here’s Mazen Haggag for Deleted Saves on Final Fantasy XVI’s ropey attempt at working in Middle Eastern and North African cultural influences.

The problem is that Dhalmekia - the only non-white nation in the base game — is all surface, no substance. It is a desert nation of craftspeople whose wealth comes from trading artisan goods across Valisthea. Much in the tradition of fantasy games, each of its towns has its own specialty goods or services: Tabor has its tanneries, Dravozd features an entire questline about its smithing, and Dalimil’s main attraction is its hot springs, which are surrounded by shops, including a carpet shop, a shisha stall, stores that sells herbs and spices, a brass ornament shop, and a bakery. For the latter, the variety tells a visual story about how the town has grown due to the captive audience of travelers enjoying the hot springs and a populace who make the most of the opportunities they get. While various objects and accoutrements on display add visual flavor, this flavor never extends to the people that occupy the country.

Lilith, of mononymic outlet Gamesline, looks at violence, games that scold you for violence, the both-sidesing of violence, and the empowerment of violence, mostly through the optics of a big stompy mech.

Armored Core 6 understands that violence is not glamorous. Death is ugly and it comes in screams and gunfire; war is filled with people who don’t get a moment to have a catchy one-liner before dying. But, depending on the route, that same violence can be cathartic. I’ve said it before: the aesthetics of death and violence are loud. Blood is bright. Some emotions are too loud to whisper. A story where a violent regime is overthrown by the downtrodden is not the same power fantasy where you uncritically protect the status quo. Both stories are violent, yet that violence is not equal.

I continuously fail to compile a Sunday Papers without someone talking sense, however sadly, about AI. Dr. Michael Cook, artificial intelligence researcher and sometime RPS contributor, remembers the optimism of earlier AI work and contrasts it with what big tech has warped it into.

I reviewed an AI paper the other day, and I'm not breaking anonymity with this description because it's one of about a dozen identical papers I've reviewed this year alone, where the core contribution was simply: we asked an LLM to do this thing. That was the paper's contribution to AI research. They took a product built by a private company and they asked it to do something, and then they reported that it did it (with no evaluation). It's perfectly okay if this is AI research now, that's fine, maybe you see value in someone reporting that they learned this was possible. Times change, words change, and if I am no longer in this field any more then I will come to accept it and find a new space to be in. But I look at papers like this today and I just find it... impossible to reconcile with the world I got excited about two decades ago. So much of AI research now is simply using the products of a handful of companies to claim they can do something. If you're lucky, they might ask another LLM to evaluate the results. The research is investigating the applications of capital, not expanding our understanding of the world.

Also on a Papers meta note: including Nathan Brown’s Hit Points is roundupping on easy mode. But it’s also one of the best, funniest, most elegantly furious newsletters in games. This one’s on the Microsoft layoffs.

Obviously no one is fooled. Sure, there’s a certain logic to, say, folding the Halo team — which has spent a lot of money, and taken a lot of time, to make pretty much the square root of fuck-all — into Activision, whose well-oiled Call Of Duty production line knows how to actually ship stuff. But I don’t think there’s a soul outside the Xbox C-suite who believes any of this is any good, or will work. The Xbox tarot deck these days consists solely of Death cards. Shuffle them all you like; it’s nice to feel busy, after all. Just don’t expect anything to change.

Bit of not-games to finish, perhaps. Here’s Niko Stratis for Paste Magazine on Nevermind’s 35th birthday.

We never really talked about the words; we just warned of what they meant. My Baptist neighbors told me they were satanic, evil even, and I learned that my feelings, those that felt at home and reflected in Cobain’s lyrics, were bad. Sinful, like pride and murder before it. My mom didn’t think much of them until he died by suicide, and when he did, his sinful lyrics became desperate warnings. We never talked about why he was sad, why he was so happy but alone, ugly but okay. We never talked about mental health, or the weight of the 1990s—a decade that is often remembered as many things, but to me it is always a little dark. It’s the brown wallpaper and dark carpet in our living room. It’s the nights that seemed to find more hours to be dark. It’s all the words I didn’t have for why Nevermind spoke to me so deeply. Why it was my favorite record to an annoying degree once it became my record, once its unknowable form became tangible to me in a way that it would never be for anyone else.

Actually, it’s not writing, but I’d be remiss not to link People Make Games’ report on Bobby Kotick’s press-targeting lawfare, a two-year (!) investigation primarily by journalist Mikhail Klimentov.

Music this week is, if you’ll forgive the lack of imagination, the Control Resonant OST. Am especially fond of whatever the fuck this is.

items.title: There Are Only Two Things That Money Can’t Buy: True Love, And Homegrown Tomatoes
items.author: Rebekah Valentine
items.summary: Everyone who knows me even somewhat closely has, in the last few years, had to listen to me gush about how much I love participating in a farm share program.
items.text:
Everyone who knows me even somewhat closely has, in the last few years, had to listen to me gush about how much I love participating in a farm share program. In winter, I pay a sizeable (but reasonable for what I get) quantity of money to a local farm to help fund their seeds and such. Then, starting in spring, every week I drive 20 minutes to that farm and am handed a big box of whatever the heck they happen to be harvesting at the time.

Fresh, local produce rules. It’s encouraged me to expand my cooking repertoire and try new foods, and I generally think everything I get tastes noticeably better than out-of-season nonsense from the big grocery store. I’ve had some of the best apples of my life this way, learned and loved the humble pawpaw fruit, and developed a begrudging respect for most greens (I still can’t get onboard with kale).

Also, tomatoes. Tomatoes! Did you know homegrown (or, well, grown at a small farm 20 minutes from home) tomatoes are…delicious?

Now, I’ve disliked tomatoes for most of my life. Watery and bland on their own, or sometimes sour or mushy and unpleasant. I avoided them if at all possible. I’ve made my views on ketchup clear elsewhere. Pasta sauce is tolerable if made well, but fresh tomatoes? Get those right out of here.

Well, what I’ve discovered from this farm share is that when you eat tomatoes fresh and in-season within spitting distance of where they’ve been grown, they’re incredible. Sure, it’s only for a few months each year, but wow! Juicy, tangy, even a little umami going on? I slice ’em and fry ’em on a cast iron and sprinkle ’em with a little Maldon seasoning salt. I toss ’em on a grilled cheese sandwich for a bit of an acidic punch. When I get lots, I cook them down into incredible pasta sauce or oven roast them with a little olive oil and mash them into salsa with some of the peppers that usually show up in the share alongside them. There are big, fat tomatoes for slicing and putting on burgers, and little grape-sized ones I can just pop in my mouth with no prep needed.

Oh, God, and if you manage to get one fresh? Right off the vine? Sun-warmed? Holy tomato, guys, what a dream!

Homegrown tomatoes! Homegrown tomatoes!

Why are we talking about tomatoes today? Well, this morning, I heard this song on the radio:

Well, you can go out to eat and that’s for sure
But it’s nothin’ a homegrown tomato won’t cure
Put ’em in a salad, put ’em in a stew
You can make your very own tomato juice
You can eat ’em with eggs, you can eat ’em with gravy
Eat ’em with beans, pinto or navy
Put ’em on the side, put ’em in the middle
Put a homegrown tomato on a hotcake griddle

This guy gets it! I can’t believe I’ve never heard this song before! “Homegrown Tomatoes” is by country singer Guy Clark, apparently one of his better-known songs, which makes it all the more embarrassing for me that I hadn’t known about it. I spend most of my time listening to sad-girl indie songs about yearning and when-will-my-husband-return-from-the-war, so the idea that you can spend a whole song rightfully extolling the virtues of the homegrown tomato has me just elated. Did you all know that you can just do that? Are there more excellent, wholesome songs about the general deliciousness of food items out there that I can listen to?

We’re unfortunately approaching the very tail end of tomato season, and I’m seeing fewer and fewer of them in my farm share each week. There were none in the most recent pick-up. It might be over. The tomato in the photo up top is the last one I have from two shares ago. I’m not even out and I miss them already.

What shall I do with this last homegrown tomato? There is, according to the very wise Guy Clark, no wrong answer:

Homegrown tomatoes, homegrown tomatoes
What’d life be without homegrown tomatoes?
Only two things that money can’t buy
And that’s true love and homegrown tomatoes

Have a lovely weekend, everyone! I hope you get to try a homegrown tomato yourself before it gets too cold for them. It’ll be a long, long winter without homegrown tomatoes, but they’ll come back again next year. They always do.

items.text:
“It’s embarrassing to know so little about something that occupies so much of your visual environment.” A little over ten minutes into his film, “The History of Concrete,” director John Wilson shares these words in praise of that very material that so many of us trample on without thinking twice. His project offers that second look, a reminder that there’s no better way to move through the world than to be guided by curiosity, bolstered by the hope that stories can be found in the most unlikely places.

Wilson operates from a place of disarming honesty and, at the start of his film, admits that the success he got from the comedy docu-series “How To with John Wilson,” like the blemishes of gum on the NYC pavement, isn’t without its blemishes. In the midst of a difficult search to find a worthy follow-up project, he attends a workshop on how to write a Hallmark movie.

After watching one film called “’Twas the Date Before Christmas,” which tried to “fit a romance inside of a topic as unromantic as affordable housing,” he decides to pair the tried and true tactics of Hallmark movies with a subject that might test the limits of their effectiveness: making a project about concrete.

As is par for the course for Wilson’s projects, his work starts as one thing and quickly finds itself off the beaten path, touching on everything from the unique grieving rituals (key words: “tattooed flesh embalming”), the terrifying infrastructures (the BQE bridge) that we have made peace living with, and ultimately, about the things in life that will last and what’s worth patching up.

For Wilson, the film continues his commitment to finding interesting stories rooted in things most people would often overlook (or, in the case of concrete, just step over). “I’m a maximalist in a lot of ways, and I think being curious makes you less bored,” he shared.

As “The History of Concrete” expands, RogerEbert.com spoke with him about humanity’s penchant for creating new grieving rituals, the virtue of curiosity, and the discernment process behind a project like this, with so many footage options to choose from.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

You port over your same “don’t show the host, only play the voice,” tactic from “How To with John Wilson.” Tell me more about your approach to narration, since when you’re recording your words, they’re divorced from where you were when you filmed the footage.

John Wilson: It can be quite fickle and dependent on mood. It’s very much a Jacob’s ladder type of process. In the case of something like my show, I usually start with a title, then try to shoot a few things relevant to the title itself.

So with something like “The History of Concrete,” I wanted to “get all the vegetables” out of the way, so to speak, which is why I included a couple of students who knew the difference between cement and concrete and could explain it. As I’m shooting, certain things will either happen to me in real life or will enter me emotionally, and I will need to write that into the script. I will look at all the footage and write a script on top of it so I’m constantly editing, writing, and shooting at the same time.

I’m wondering about how you choose to match footage with your words because the ways in which what we see on-screen contradicts what’s spoken–and when they align–are fascinating to take note of. The scene where you talk about the poor foundations of buildings like your gym is “making people really upset because the city doesn’t seem to acknowledge the problem.” You intersperse that with a humorous video of someone mollywopping an exercise ball.

That’s an example where it helps to have something as uniquely specific as that visual to build around. I started with this desire to use the shot of the gym flooding, then I was thinking, “Okay, what else do I have from this environment?” That is kind of the template I use for the sequences you see in the film going forward: I have a kernel of an idea, and then I try to either find something I already have or shoot something new that adds a punchline. I try to use the rule of threes when I can when writing certain sequences, but you don’t always need a punchline at the same time.

On that note of discernment, you talked about how, when making a feature, there are no time constraints apart from “consideration for the audience.” With your show, you were constrained by the straitjacket of twenty-eight minutes, but what guides you and editor Cori Wapnowska’s process when you have a cornucopia of footage to work with?

That first cut is really messy and has everything in it, and when I’m looking at what I’ve assembled, I am able to see the whole picture, where the actual emotional turns are and what the plot is. That version of the film also helps me determine which strong sequences, in isolation, I can build the film around and what can support the crescendo to those moments.

I try not to have any redundant revelations or ideas in the film. The temptation can be to double up, but I try to hold fast to that. If I repeat any beats, I want to reveal slightly different information in whatever comes next. For the most part, even if an interview feels like a non-sequitur, it needs to rhyme with something else in the film, or its inclusion needs to strengthen the film thematically by reinforcing a particular metaphor.

For example, there’s that sequence where I document a military exercise that takes place out of a high school at one point. You can take that as just an observation that I happened to tag on, but some of the intentionality there was to show how that fits in with this recurring theme of rule-following, our obsession with structure and order, and what it is about ourselves as a species that we feel a need to be told what to do.

Beyond those questions, one thing that felt like it unified “The History of Concrete” was your documentation of how people cannot help but use rituals to process grief and loss. It’s such a small part of the film, but I’m struck by that community that held a vigil for the fish that were killed when their pond was filled with concrete.

Yeah, I mean, we showcase Chef Boyardee’s grave here. I think death and fatality is a kind of recurring background theme in a lot of the work that I end up making. I think that there can be the death of a physical person, but I think there’s the death of civic space and these larger industries around us all the time, and we have different ceremonies for that. It feels like the new public ceremony is almost “protest for mourning.”

I feel like there are cultures that just kind of put you in a pine box, and it’s very unflashy, but then you have this industry of tattoo preservation where it feels like you’re mummifying somebody. I like, I’m constantly debating in my own life whether or not I should be sad about something disappearing or if I should be trying to figure out ways emotionally to deal with the disappearance of something. Looking at the different ways that other cultures grieve is a big part of that education.

Doesn’t it feel overwhelming, though, to know how to properly lament when it feels like the scale of things we should mourn for outstrips our ability to comprehend what we might be losing?

Yes, but this movie is dealing with a thousand-year timeline. I’m trying to acknowledge humans as grains of sand in this endless, infinite time. I try not to zoom out too far just because I need to keep the point sharpened to a degree.

It makes me think, though: what does a thousand-year city look like? How are we to live our lives on Earth knowing that we only have so much time here? It seems like many people’s answer is to engage in cyclical behavior. Is that something market forces determine and force on us, or something we naturally do to get through existing? I wonder if there’s a better way.

It ties back to that line your subject mentions about the BQE’s crumbling infrastructure: “We’re aware of a flaw but are incapable of stopping it.”

But are we really incapable of stopping it? I ultimately try to contain myself within a timeline that I can mentally comprehend, but that yields its own interesting challenges. It’s funny, because I was talking to the people who were in the tattoo preservation business, and I asked a couple of people in different interviews that weren’t in the movie, essentially, “What do you plan to do with this [business] after you pass away?” There’s no plan for that.

It becomes this act of kicking the can of preservation and legacy just further down the road. think people tend to think within a hundred years of their life, usually, or maybe even less. I think that’s mostly what you can comprehend because when you start to think about 10,000 years from now, it’s just like, “Why am I doing anything?”

When I look at your projects and the way you deploy humor, you often use it as a kind of weapon to subvert the dynamics of who holds power. By highlighting the absurdity of our existence, your humor calls into question the aforementioned market forces that shape our lives. How do you feel this idea has expanded with a project like “The History of Concrete?”

I think about that all the time. I try to be right on the razor’s edge as often as I can of what’s okay and what’s not, because I think that’s where a lot of the best comedy and art lies. I think humor can be an instrument to speak truth to power, and if I’m punching, I always try to punch up. I think there are some obvious villains out in the world that everyone can usually laugh at, whether it’s a cop doing something funny or even just the mayor, no matter how popular the mayor is. I think it’s pretty timeless to have an antagonistic relationship with the mayor in certain ways for a lot of New Yorkers.

Landlords too, which, as you’re a landlord, speaks to your willingness to fall on the blade yourself.

Yeah; I occupy a complicated place within the city that I acknowledge, and I try to lacerate myself in equal measure to a lot of the people within capital “P” politics.

I’m speaking to you in the middle of TIFF, and there’s a film that premiered, “Babies,” where a character played by Seth Rogen critiques the ways we praise babies for being “curious” when the only reason they’re curious is that they don’t know anything.

(Laughs) Yeah, I can relate.

That connects in some ways to what I feel is the thematic spine of this project because you say this line. “Once you’re used to something, it becomes kind of hard to change your lifestyle without external pressure.” It’s so easy to move through the world, simply accepting things as they are, and we lose that childlike curiosity. What helps you stay curious?

I tend to try to just run in a direction that nobody else is running in. I feel like I can’t work fast enough a lot of the time. There are just so many interesting and funny things to comment on and to explore within human relationships, and humanity’s relationship with the environment. You can literally pick anything … you can throw a dart at a board of words and just pick one, and then that’s your new obsession. You can find a galaxy within any one of those things.

There are a lot of things I want to see fixed in the city. I think a lot of New Yorkers have a signature thing they gripe about, and it ends up consuming their lives. Making art about something you would like to see improved will never get old.

In so many ways, I think part of me feels like I accidentally made this movie, and other parts of me feel like it was always meant to happen. I think it’s surreal that we’re talking about it right now and that what I’ve crafted is in any condition to analyze. I’m a maximalist in a lot of ways, and I think being curious makes you less bored. It makes you actually understand your environment rather than just passively walking through it.

Waking up from the matrix can be frustrating, but it’s also cool because it connects you with other people. I don’t know; meeting the world with your curiosity renews your faith in humanity in a certain way and helps you engage in things that you weren’t engaged in before.

items.text:
The year might be drawing to a close, but it's a perfect time to do something new with your Japanese study! Take a look below at the latest list of Japanese learning resources, lovingly selected by our team, to help supercharge your Japanese study.

Activate Your Japanese!

Activate Your Japanese! is a 24-episode drama about a Vietnamese girl named Xuan who came to Japan to work in a hotel. It comes from Japan's national broadcasting network, known as NHK, which is known for producing quality video content about all sorts of topics. You can think of them as the BBC or CNN of Japan. In the drama, she encounters a sentient keychain, new friends, and lots of new Japanese. And as with any drama, there are elements of humor and romance that really make it entertaining.

Each video is divided into parts: The main skit, Today's Strategy, Onomatopoeia, and Welcome to My Japan. The main skit follows Xuan and her time adjusting to Japanese life, all while providing useful communication strategies. Next, the Today's Strategy section focuses on a useful communication strategy or phrase that Xuan utilized in the main skit. Plenty of examples are provided, making this part of each video particularly useful for learners. Then comes the Onomatopoeia bit, which introduces a common Japanese onomatopoeia. Again, several examples are provided to help reinforce how the word is used in real life. And finally, the Welcome to My Japan bit finishes off each video with a presentation of someone's life after coming to Japan. Many of these individuals immigrated to Japan for work and have lived in the country for several years. Their work, interests, and hobbies are highlighted in this section.

Every video in this series comes with translated captions and even a transcript, making it ideal for learners at level who want to practice reading or listening skills. But even if learning Japanese is not your main goal, the series can still be enjoyed purely as a drama for one's own entertainment. According to the site, this series will be available until 2027, so there's plenty of time to go through each of the 15-minute episodes.

Beyond Activate Your Japanese!, the NHK has a number of other resources for Japanese learners, like the Essential Japanese section, which provides survival phrases, and Easy Japanese: Conversation Lessons, which contains lots of learning content related to conversation practice. There's something for everyone, so check it out!

あかね的日本語教室

VIDEO

あかね的日本語教室, otherwise known as Akane's Japanese Class, is a popular YouTube channel produced by a Japanese teacher named Akane. This channel is targeted towards intermediate and advanced learners. However, Akane mentions that this channel is also accessible to beginners who want a bit of a challenge. The difficulty comes from all the videos being entirely in Japanese. The subtitles at the bottom of the screen are in Japanese, and include furigana over more difficult kanji. There are also closed captioning subtitles that can be turned off and on, with an impressive number of languages covered — 15!

The videos on this channel are very educational while also entertaining. The topics surround learning Japanese, travel around Japan, everyday life in Japan, and more. An example of Akane's videos that Japanese learners may find most useful are "[Business Japanese] Basics of telephone correspondence" and several interviews with non-native speakers living in Japan and studying the language. Each video lasts about 10-15 minutes in length, and they go by quickly. Because Akane speaks slowly, it's easy to follow the dialogue. If you're looking for even more content by Akane, you can also check out the podcast and Instagram page she also has.

Japanese Immersion with Asami

Japanese Immersion with Asami is a YouTube channel that, as the name suggests, focuses on teaching via comprehensible input; that is, Japanese made as easy to understand as possible, even for beginners, without relying on English explanations or translations. Asami has been a Japanese teacher since 2015, and with her trusty partner Hyougen, mostly reads stories in her videos, with helpful explanations and commentary; all in Japanese.

The videos are a great way to get your feet wet engaging with Japanese media more, without feeling like you're alone in the endeavor. In fact, the casual, supportive atmosphere of her videos might be their best feature; it really does feel like a private lesson. And with several series in a variety of genres and titles, such as Kiki's Delivery Service and short stories, you're sure to find a narrative that piques your interest.

日本語表現インフォ

One of the most difficult parts of learning another language can be expressions. As language conveys culture, each individual language has different expressions relevant to its own culture, and translating between them is no easy task. Thankfully for Japanese learners, there's the helpful website 日本語表現インフォ, or "Japanese Expression Info" to make things a little easier.

The site is very straightforward, with various expressions grouped into different categories, like expressions conveying emotions, sensations, or people, for example. From there they're often broken down even further, like expressions relevant to conveying different degrees of sadness.

Not only will using these sorts of expressions add a sense of naturalness to your own writing, but they might help you while reading Japanese. 日本語表現インフォ is a great resource for learning both Japanese language and culture.

Sail is a unique approach to Japanese language exchange apps. Available on iOS and Android, Japanese learners first register for an account, filling out some of their interests and a basic self-introduction. But rather than connect with teachers or other language learners, Sail connects you to native Japanese speakers in the form of retirees and senior citizens. Like all similar apps, you're able to look at the profiles of various exchange partners, and find someone who might be a good fit in terms of interests and availability. Conversations are set to last 25 minutes, offering a contained experience: long enough that you're able to actually chat, but not so long that you might run out of steam.

It's a unique concept, and one that works well. Older people make good conversation partners, and are often very cordial and have a lot of free time. They're excited to get the chance to connect to learners, and share something of their language and culture, and this eagerness is contagious. What's even better is that Sail allows for unlimited conversations for a simple fee of $14.90 a month, with discounts at longer terms. This makes Sail one of the best bangs for your buck for Japanese learners hoping to converse.

items.text:
Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?

items.text:
Mario Harik is the CEO of XPO, one of the largest logistics companies in the world.

For years, he was the protege of legendary entrepreneur Brad Jacobs (who built eight multibillion-dollar companies from scratch). Today, Mario leads 40,000 people with a management style shaped by what he learned. It’s a rare combination of smart capital allocation, discipline, deep listening, and a genuine belief in human potential.

Mario shares how he uses real-time data and second-order thinking to make better decisions faster, how he hires and develops A players (and the test that instantly tells you who isn’t one), how he runs meetings that pull the best thinking out of the most junior person in the room, what he learned working alongside one of the best entrepreneurs of our generation, and why ego, complacency, and small goals are quietly capping everything.

I hope you enjoy this conversation as much as I did.

Featured clips

Letting go of perfection and understanding how people operate

Learning from frontline employees and feedback loops

Analytical approach to risk and decision-making

Creating a high-performance environment through belief and feedback

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript

+ Check out the Granola notes.

Tiny Lessons

“If you set big goals, you achieve great things. If you set small goals, you achieve small things.”

“Ego is thinking you’re so good at something that you stop learning.”

“I worry if I’m in a team meeting and everybody’s aligned on a solution.”

In meetings, senior people speak last.

“A lot of leaders spend time on the output. You’ve got to spend time on the inputs.”

Tell people what to do but not how. When you tell them how, you set the ceiling at your best idea not theirs.

If somebody quits and your feeling is ‘whew, that’s good news’ — you should have gotten rid of them long ago.

“Most people think at the speed of speech. You can train your mind to go much faster.”

“When I give constructive feedback, I never make it subjective. I always ground it on data.”

“A lot of what people flag as potential issues ends up being why somebody fails at work.”

Yearly performance reviews are theater. “Performance reviews should be done on a daily and weekly basis.”

Don’t stop at the first answer. Double and triple-click.

The three variables that matter most when hiring: “Are they good at what they do? Are they serious about work? Are they kind?”

“It’s okay to have some friction.”

“Disagree all you want. Just focus on the problem, not the person.”

“Winning breeds winning.”

“Life is short. You’ve got to set big, big goals.”

“If you want to create alpha, don’t settle for a local maximum.”

“My hobbies are my work and my kids.”

“Every morning you have a choice: do the job the way you always do it, or learn new things.”

The only competition is yourself. “The bar isn’t beating the competition. The bar is: are we achieving the best we can achieve?”

“Work is part of life, the same way life is part of work.”

“When you show someone you believe in them, they have much higher odds of being great.”

“Every person in their own way is beautiful. Your job is to find how their mind works, not flatten it.”

“The biggest lever in business is who’s on the team and how they work with each other.”

The anticuchos at Cholapink. | Cholapink

We’ve been covering various NYC restaurants, food, drinks, bars, etc. news intel over on our daily newsletter (please sign up if you haven’t already!), but we’re also making it easier for everyone to catch up by rounding ‘em up here every week (check out August, July, and June’s).

September 11

A new Peruvian spot from a chef and a rapper

Peruvian chef Jaime Pesaque (of notable Lima restaurant Mayta) and Puerto Rican rapper Daddy Yankee (yes) are teaming up to open a new fast-casual Peruvian restaurant in New York City this fall. Cholapink is opening at 32 Spring Street, near Mott Street, in Nolita in October. The menu highlights grilled street food, also known as anticuchos, with ajis (marinades and sauces) like miso-glazed chicken thighs, pineapple gochujang pork belly, yuzu-amarillo fish, and spicy peanut mushrooms.

An NYC taco fave gets private equity funding

NYC’s favorite taqueria chain Los Tacos No. 1 is getting investment money from private equity firm TSG Consumer Partners, as reported by QSR. After the news was announced, people took to commenting on Los Tacos’ Instagram page, worrying about potential quality issues and increased prices (see: the discourse about Salt Hank’s acquisition by food hall behemoth Wonder). The team responded, assuring that they’re “definitely not messing with the tacos,” and that the reason they took the investment is so that they can “keep getting better at it” and expand. The restaurant recently partnered with Gap on an apparel collaboration.

An NYC artist and restaurant owner has died

Lucien Smith, the NYC artist who had revived iconic Chinatown restaurant Food, has died at the age of 37, as reported by Cultured. The restaurant had posted last week that it was temporarily closing.

Fall restaurant season is HERE

Bad news: Summer is unofficially over. Good news: it’s fall preview season! Part one of Eater NY’s most anticipated restaurant openings of the fall is on the website; part two is over on Substack.

An anticipated Hong Kong-style diner finds its address

Turns out chef Lucas Sin is indeed opening his dream cha chaan teng Lok Kee at M Star Cafe in Chinatown, where he’d been popping up this late summer.

Mrs. and Mr. Swift’s NYC night out

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce dined at Ambassadors Clubhouse on Saturday, September 6, per a rep for the fancy Indian restaurant in Nomad. They dined in one of the private dining rooms, enjoying drinks and food. I’d bet they ordered the tableside whiskey cocktail, the Patiala Peg.

Top Chef winner pops up with bodega preview

Chef Danny Garcia continues previewing his forthcoming Latin halal restaurant, Only Goods, with a pop-up bodega this weekend. It’s taking place at 307 Bedford Avenue, near South Second Street in Williamsburg on Saturday, September 12, from 1 to 5 p.m.

A kaiseki anniversary party

Tribeca kaiseki Muku is celebrating its first anniversary with a special tasting menu this fall, featuring dishes like a rare Japanese sweetfish and harako meshi, a dish of white rice, salmon, and roe. The $375 menu is available through Saturday, October 3.

A 10-year-restaurant collab celebration

To celebrate Fish Cheek’s 10th birthday, the restaurant is teaming up with other NYC restaurants and bars for special collaboration dishes. Starting on Saturday, September 12, find the choo chee michelada and zapp popcorn chicken at Lower East Side cocktail bar Double Chicken Please; the razor clams with nam jim seafood at American Asian Hudson Square restaurant Kiko; the clam pie at both the East Village and Bushwick locations of Ops Pizza; and sliced flaky Thai coconut cake at sibling gluten-free Nolita bakery Bub’s. And then, starting on Monday, September 14, there’s a special burger at Prospect Heights Jewish bistro Gertrude’s.

September 4

A Vietnamese American bakery returns to Brooklyn

Some good news: After baker Doris Hồ-Kane shuttered her Vietnamese American bakery in February, she’s working on bringing back Bạn Bè to its original Carroll Gardens neighborhood.

Hồ-Kane launched a Kickstarter campaign to help fund the opening. She’s aiming to open in November at 115 Columbia Street, at Kane Street, in the Columbia Street Waterfront District.

The resurrected space will have a takeout window and a first-time indoor dine-in space. On deck are pastries and sweets like the beautiful bright-green pandan honeycomb cake and new stuff like pandan lime madeleines and pandan chocolate tiramisu. For savory vegeterian items, look for banh mi, Vietnamese crepes, and summer rolls, along with coffee and tea drinks.

The McNally son ventures into the restaurant world

Keith McNally’s son, George, opens his Tribeca restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3, at 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable.

Buy stellar baked goods for a good cause

Expert baker Natasha Pickowicz is hosting a community bake sale this weekend to raise money for Queens nonprofit Make the Road New York. Our Little Bake Sale features chefs like Pickowicz herself, Zoë Kanan of Elbow Bread, Morgan Knight of Saint Street Cakes, Flynn McCarry of Cove, Ali Domrongchai, and many others. It’s free to attend; each pastry is worth one ticket, which is $10. The event, which is a partnership with indie food publication Cake Zine, takes place on Sunday, September 6, from 3 to 5 p.m. at Little Island, the park on Pier 55 along Hudson River Park at West 13th Street.

Two NYC restaurants take over Times Square Red Lobster

A restaurant group behind NYC restaurants, including American brasserie the Smith and pizzeria Parla, is taking over the recently shuttered Red Lobster in Times Square, as reported by the New York Post. The business plans to open a fifth location of the Smith and a pizza-slice spinoff of Parla at a two-floor address at 582 Seventh Avenue, between West 41st and 42nd streets, set to debut in 2028.

A bread bakery grows in Crown Heights

In more bakery news, Apt. 2 Bread, a micro-bakery best known for its focaccia, is working on opening a bread-focused bakery named Boots Bread in Crown Heights. Carla Finley is teaming up with Megan Wang for the new venture. When the bakery opens, expect all sorts of breads made with regional grains.

What’s happening with Food?

Looks like Chinatown restaurant Food, the revitalized Chinatown restaurant now run by artist Lucien Smith, seems to have “closed until further notice,” per its Instagram.

A Radio Bakery branch is temporarily closed

The Greenpoint location of Radio Bakery is temporarily closing for renovations, from Tuesday, September 1, through Monday, September 21. To help ease the demand, the Prospect Heights location is staying open later (until 6 p.m.) through Sunday, September 13.

An Austin bar pop-up worth going to

One of my personal favorite bars ever, Austin’s Nickel City, is coming to New York City for a pop-up this month. Owner Travis Tober is taking over the bar of Romeo’s in the East Village, on Wednesday, September 9, from 8 to 11 p.m., with Dr Pepper Old Fashioneds, Mexican martinis, and more.

If you’re going to Harry Styles…

If your Labor Day weekend plans include seeing Harry Styles at Madison Square Garden this Friday, September 4, and/or Saturday, September 5, we’ve got a handy guide for you, at least when it comes to drinking and eating. Pro tip: Make sure you’re seated/standing by the time opener Jamie XX plays his final song, because Harry and company take the stage at the same time to kick off the show.
